In the Head Start Impact Study, children offered Head Start were twice as likely as controls to use a center-based program in spring 2003.

This randomized-study finding concerns the early care arrangement produced by an offer of Head Start, not a comparison with no alternative services. The report includes Head Start, preschool and child care in its center-based category.

The final report describes end-of-program-year impacts for the randomized access comparison. It does not justify treating every measured outcome, later follow-up, or implementation setting as favorable.
The Head Start Impact Study found favorable cognitive and health impacts after one program year, with more significant findings for the 3-year-old cohort.
The Head Start Impact Study compared Head Start access with a mix of alternative care arrangements, not with a universal no-service condition.

About 17% of the 3-year-old control group and 14% of the 4-year-old control group entered Head Start during the first year; the report therefore distinguishes intent-to-treat access estimates from estimates adjusted for no-shows and crossovers.
By the end of first grade, the Head Start Impact Study found few statistically significant differences for the sample as a whole.

The report follows children from program entry through first grade and reports this result for the randomized groups as a whole. It does not establish that every subgroup, unmeasured outcome, or later-life outcome was zero.
